messages:
john.cust: Hey team — our app started getting 429s and a billing spike around 10:02 UTC. We have 100 worker containers hitting the Redwood API via a shared API key through our proxy. Curious if this is an org-level quota or per-key / per-IP enforcement. Our dashboard shows a 'quota exhausted' alert but the project-level quota shouldn't be reached. Any idea?

maya (support): Thanks for the report — can you paste the 429 response body (if any) and whether the requests were coming from the same public IP or many? Also, which auth method are you using (API key vs OAuth service account)?

john.cust: Here's the response we logged from one of the failing requests: 
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "error": {
    "type": "rate_limit",
    "message": "quota exceeded",
    "scope": "unknown",
    "retry_after": 27
  }
}
```
Requests were NAT'd through our k8s cluster egress IP (single public IP). We are using a single shared API key for all containers. The project's quota is 1M tokens/day and we were at ~720k at the time. Billing dashboard shows a sudden token spike + burst charges.

alex (eng-sre): A couple of things to check: 1) whether your API key is scoped to a specific project or to the org, 2) whether any extra upstream proxy-level rate limiting exists that counts per-IP, and 3) if there are short-window burst limits (per-second) that aren't reflected in daily quota graphs. Do you have any logs from our edge (X-Request-ID) or the proxy?

john.cust: We have our proxy logs. Example request headers we forward: 
```
POST /v1/generate HTTP/1.1
Host: api.redwood.ai
Authorization: Bearer rk_live_XXX
User-Agent: myapp/1.2.3
X-Forwarded-For: 54.21.12.33
X-Project-ID: proj-abc123
```
We don't set an X-Org-ID header. The proxy rewrites auth but does not attach any Redwood-specific org header.

sam (eng-infra): If you're using a single live key across many containers and all egress through one IP, two enforcement layers could bite: the API key quota (per-key or per-project) and an IP-based burst limiter at the edge that prevents very high req/s from a single IP. Our docs: short-window burst throttles are enforced to protect multi-tenant edges — they're separate from daily token quotas.

dave (billing): On the billing side I can see a transient spike of token usage at 10:01–10:03 UTC for your org id (we map usage by both project and org). There are two possible causes: a) one of your containers looped and re-sent requests, or b) the proxy retried idempotently and doubled tokens. My note: org-level accounting aggregated across projects can trigger an 'org quota' alert even if an individual project is below its own quota.

john.cust: So is the 429 coming from org-level quota or from IP burst policing? The response didn't include "scope: org" or similar.

alex (eng-sre): The response payload you pasted shows "scope": "unknown" — that typically means the edge rejected before mapping the key to a project/org (common when required headers are missing or the auth lookup hit the cache expiry). Two concrete repro checks: 1) hit the API directly from your laptop using the same API key (bypassing proxy) and see if 429 persists; 2) rotate to a different API key pegged to the same project and test. If direct calls succeed but proxied calls 429, likely IP-burst limiter or proxy mis-aggregation.

maya (support): Can you run this quick curl test (replace API_KEY and change to your public IP check):
```
curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer API_KEY" \
     -H "User-Agent: smoke-test" \
     -d '{"prompt":"hi","max_tokens":5}' \
     https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate
```
Also attach the full proxied request logs + any X-Request-IDs we can correlate to edge logs.

john.cust: Ran direct curl from my laptop (different public IP) — got a 200. Then reran the same curl via our proxy (same API key) and got 429. Proxy logs show bursts of 120–150 req/s for a short period.

ratebot: [automated] correlated edge logs for request IDs: rqd_00123 -> 429, rqd_00124 -> 429, rqd_00150 -> 200 (different IP). Edge note: 'per-ip short-window limit triggered' at 2024-10-01T10:02:05Z for ip=54.21.12.33.

sam (eng-infra): That nails it — per-IP short-window limiter. Your single egress IP produces high instantaneous throughput. Two remediation paths: 1) enable connection pooling + jittered backoff in workers to smooth req/s, or 2) switch to per-worker API keys (so rate limiters see distributed keys rather than aggregated IP). If you cannot spawn multiple egress IPs, per-key distribution is the most reliable.

john.cust: If we create multiple API keys and rotate them across workers, will billing / quotas still be correct? We don't want to split the project's quota unintentionally.

dave (billing): Billing aggregates at org/project levels. Creating multiple API keys within the same project will still draw from the same project/org token pool unless you explicitly create keys isolated to another project. So token accounting and daily quotas remain consistent — the limiter behavior will change because the edge applies some checks per-key as well.

alex (eng-sre): Quick note on scoping semantics that often causes confusion: 
- API key scoping: keys can be project-scoped or org-scoped depending on how they were created.
- Daily quotas: typically applied at project or org level (configurable per-customer contract).
- Short-window rate limits: often applied at multiple dimensions (per-key, per-ip, per-region) and those are independent of daily token quotas.

maya (support): For your immediate unblock, try two things: 1) create 3 ephemeral API keys under the same project and stagger worker request starts, 2) implement client-side small random sleep (2–20ms) before heavy calls to avoid synchronized bursts. We'll keep monitoring.

john.cust: We created 4 keys and started round-robin assignment across pods. After a 10 minute warm-up the 429s stopped and latency returned to normal. Billing shows the token spike and then normalizes. Thanks — what should we change long-term?

alex (eng-sre): Long-term options: (a) if you need high sustained req/s from one IP, request a network-tier exception with our infra team (requires justification + SLA change), (b) adopt multiple egress IPs (NAT pool), or (c) use service account OAuth tokens tied to per-worker identities so limits are applied per-identity. We'll open an internal infra ticket if you want an exception.

dave (billing): I'll mark the billing spike as "investigated; caused by burst from shared proxy" and flag it for potential one-time adjustment if you have supporting logs (we can consider crediting for accidental double-billing in narrow cases). Send the X-Request-IDs and proxy timestamps.

maya (support): Copying next steps: 1) john to upload proxy logs + X-Request-IDs (you already pasted some, but include full batches), 2) eng-infra (sam) to evaluate network-tier exception (+ticket link), 3) billing (dave) will review for possible one-time credit. Reopen thread if 429s recur. :thumbsup:

john.cust: Uploaded full logs to the ticket. One last edge question — if we switch to per-worker keys, is there any auth edgecase where the proxy could leak a 'org' attribution and cause the per-key limits to be bypassed?

alex (eng-sre): Not really — attribution is deterministic: key->project/org mapping is authoritative. The edge will always resolve the key to the project or org it belongs to. The only leakage vector is if your proxy rewrites Authorization headers or reuses a different key in retries. Keep retries idempotent and preserve original headers.

john.cust: Great, thanks everyone. I'll monitor and close when billing looks normal.

maya (support): Thanks — closing scope for now but will reopen if you see anything else.
